claim_verdicts.reason: C1-E1 gives every condition in the claim (waiting share, long-held connections, listener/upstream behavior, scheduling, filter nonblocking-ness); C1-E2 says a CPU-intensive filter on the loop can hurt unrelated requests and that swapping the library cannot speed cryptography, serialization or business logic.

C2-E1 says CPU efficiency did not materially improve for the API-facing, computation-heavier cluster; C2-E2 says the lower-work logging cluster saw about 25% throughput improvement with associated CPU-use reduction. Number, populations and direction match.

C3-E1 states the trade from per-request stacks to callback lifecycle state, context propagation and manual resource cleanup; C3-E2 names ByteBuf leaks, file-descriptor leaks and dropped responses as failures of incomplete async error paths.

C4-E1 says downstream latency and repeated retries can amplify open connections, threads, memory and scheduler pressure; C4-E2 says an asynchronous interface does not make the receiver infinitely fast; the added async failure modes are stated by C3-E2 in the same ledger.

C5-E1 gives the moderate-connection, all-CPU-heavy, latency-met, simplicity condition; C5-E2 gives the worker-pool mixed design with explicit budgets; C5-E3 gives the separate comparison of waiting capacity, CPU per request class and p99 under saturation.

C6-E1 lists the blocking detector, bounded offload executor, context and principal propagation, deadline/cancellation cleanup, leak detection, retry/admission limits and cohort-level p99; C6-E2 adds the known rollback version.
C7-E1 says blocking on JDBC, a mutex or an HTTP response prevents unrelated operations on that loop from progressing; C7-E2 says a nonblocking stack does not make blocking JDBC nonblocking.
C8-E1 warns against equating async code with parallelism and names shared connection pools, global locks, fan-in serialization and constrained executors as serial bottlenecks.
C9-E1 lists the four distinct guarantees; C9-E2 says a timeout signal is not proof the underlying blocking operation was interrupted; C9-E3 says a ThreadLocal correlation ID may disappear or leak.

C10-E1 separates persistent-connection scalability from a uniform CPU-efficiency win; C10-E2/E3 require separating response time from resource service demand with the 300 ms / 4 ms CPU / 40 ms DB example; C10-E4 rejects aggregate throughput as a rollback criterion.
C11-E1 lists active connections/threads, carrier pinning, event-loop stalls, canceled and retried requests, CPU per operation, p99 by class, queue age and dead-letter counts.
C12-E1 specifies equivalent open-loop offered load, bounded concurrency, the injected faults and the recorded metrics; C12-E2 adds canary by class at matched traffic.
C13-E1 says a closed generator reduces offered load when the system stalls; C13-E2 requires offered/admitted/completed rates separately; C13-E3 says the backlog can be hidden.
C14-E1 states each rejection and insufficient-evidence condition named in the claim.
C15-E1/E2/E3 state the critical-component operability condition and name bypass, configuration drift, stale routes, quota failure and a total backend-blocking outage as the failure modes.
C16-E1 says a model that hides rejection can report a high success rate while refusing work at the front door; C16-E2 says the timeout rate is the dominant failure mode.
C17-E2 names the rehearsed rollback that completes inside the observation window; C17-E1/E3 say these are measurements and operational evidence, not model parameters.
C18-E1 calls developer and operational cost a narrative trade-off, not measured engineering hours; C18-E2 calls retry-storm resilience some benefit requiring tuning, not a zero-failure guarantee.
C19-E1 says a socket timeout is not a complete request deadline; C19-E2 says cancellation is not proof a previously committed effect was undone.
C20-E1/E2 are the table rows for CPU sampling missing waiting states and wall-clock sampling carrying overhead, thread-grouping and signal/runtime limits.
C21-E1 makes bounded platform threads a defensible initial decision for CPU-heavy work; C21-E2 forbids CPU-intensive crypto or JDBC on Netty event loop. C21-E1 scope is a gRPC worker pool.

C22-E1 says bulkhead bypass, undersized partitions and a shared hidden queue defeat isolation and requires per-pool queue age, utilization and rejected work to be detected and the class failed explicitly.

claim_verdicts.reason: C1-E1 defines service capacity as the rate the pool can complete when busy; C1-E2 defines utilization as offered load divided by capacity.
Core claim 1: C2-E1 gives 12 / 0.5 = 24 requests per second and 20 / 24 = 0.833; C2-E2 confirms the arithmetic for the synthetic case.
Core claim 2: C3-E1/E2/E3 are the worked-comparison rows for A, B and C, each at capacity 24 with arrival 20, and C at p95 1.769; the 18-server/0.75 s equality follows from the row and C2-E1 formula.
Core claim 3: C4-E1 names service-time confusion as dividing mean service time by servers in the wrong direction, producing capacity too high or too low.
C5-E1 says average CPU utilization is not comparable across different server counts unless cost and work units are stated; C5-E2 requires a direction and unit for every metric.

C6-E1 fixes the Poisson 20 rps workload over 1,800 s after 300 s warmup with 30 replications and seed base 20261029; C6-E2 fixes C at 18 servers, 0.75 s mean service, 120-request queue, 1.5 s timeout, two attempts, linear backoff and cost 14.0; C6-E3 makes the candidate configuration the intended variable.
C7-E1/E2/E3 give A p95 0.870 cost 1.81, B p95 1.206 cost 1.34, and C p95 1.769 cost 3.63 with success 0.9679 and timeout 0.111.

C8-E1/E2 give C two attempts, retry amplification 1.079, timeout 0.111 and success 0.9679; C8-E3 says retries raise service load above offered load; C8-E4 attributes the higher B p95 to waiting longer before timing out.

Core claim 4 as supplied: C9-E1/E2 set the 3.0 cost and 1.5 s p95 hard ceilings and C9-E3 eliminates C on both, which supports the elimination half only. No supplied quote states the saturation-run figures (utilization 1.0, throughput 24, rejection 0.2, 77.6-request backlog) or the capacity-versus-realized-throughput distinction, and the answer does not report them.
C10-E1 says a hard constraint eliminates a candidate even with the highest success rate; C10-E3 names constraint laundering.

C13-E1 lists the metric set; C13-E2 says the checkout model has no dependency calls or storage; C13-E4/E5 say the gates do not establish a match to a real system or production behavior.
C14-E1 to E3 mark arrival rate, service mean and servers as assumed; C14-E4 gives the reversal triggers above 22 rps or 0.65 s.

C15-E1 gives C retry amplification 1.079 and timeout 0.111; C15-E2 gives the capacity/utilization arithmetic; C15-E3 gives C p95 and success; the 21.6 attempts and 0.90 utilization are arithmetic on these quotes.
C16-E1 gives capacity 24 at arrival 20 and utilization 0.833; C16-E2 is C row showing capacity 24; the 4 rps spare-capacity figure follows arithmetically.

C17-E1 gives service-mean sensitivity 0.536/0.639 against arrival-rate 0.361/0.464 and the quadratic-screen caveat; C17-E2/E3 say it does not prove production dominance and is used to direct measurement.

C18-E1 labels mu as the pool requests-per-second capacity while C18-E2 writes utilization as lambda/mu for one server; C18-E3 resolves the arithmetic as capacity = servers divided by mean service time.
